prompt: Which of these creatures is NOT an insect?
hint: Insects have six legs, but spiders have eight!

fact.text: Spiders and tarantulas are arachnids with eight legs, while every true insect has six legs!
fact.support: Garden spiders are eight-legged arachnids, whereas all true insects have six legs.

misconception: Thinking spiders are insects because both are tiny creepy-crawlies with many legs.

prompt: Which of these wild meadow wonders is NOT a plant?
hint: Mushrooms are fungi, so they cannot make their own food from sunlight.

fact.text: Mushrooms are fungi with a stem and cap, which cannot make food from sunlight like green plants do!
fact.support: Mushrooms are fungi that absorb nutrients from wood, while plants create food with sunlight.

misconception: Thinking mushrooms are plants because they grow in forest dirt and have stems.

prompt: Tap all the animals that lay eggs in nests or soil!
hint: Look for the turtle with a shell and the soaring eagle.

fact.text: Female turtles bury their eggs in sand or soil to hatch in warmth!
fact.support: Mother turtles bury their eggs in sandy soil so their babies can hatch.

misconception: Thinking all furry land animals lay eggs like birds and reptiles do.

prompt: Tap all the creatures that can fly!
hint: Butterflies, bees, and even furry bats have wings for flying!

fact.text: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly; flying squirrels only glide.
fact.support: Bats have winged hands that flap, making them the only mammals capable of true flight.

misconception: Thinking flying squirrels fly with wings instead of just gliding through the air.

prompt: Order the stages of this winged insect's life cycle from the start!
hint: Start from egg, hatch to caterpillar, form chrysalis, then emerge flying.

fact.text: Butterflies go through complete metamorphosis in four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, and adult!
fact.support: An insect begins as a tiny egg, hatches into a caterpillar, rests in a chrysalis, and emerges as a butterfly.

misconception: Thinking caterpillars turn straight into flying butterflies without resting inside a chrysalis.

prompt: Order how a little plant grows up into a lovely bloom!
hint: Begin with the seed in soil and finish with the bloom.

fact.text: When a seed germinates, a root sprouts downward first, followed by a green shoot growing upward toward the light!
fact.support: A planted seed germinates in soil, pushes out a tiny sprout, grows a green stem, and opens into a sunflower.

misconception: Thinking leaves and flowers bloom before a seed grows roots into the soil.

prompt: Which planet is the hottest planet in our solar system?
hint: Mercury is closest, but Venus traps extreme heat under thick clouds.

fact.text: Venus is the hottest planet in our solar system because its atmosphere traps heat!
fact.support: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps intense solar heat.

misconception: Thinking Mercury is the hottest planet just because it is closest to the Sun.

prompt: What kind of space object is our warm daytime Sun?
hint: The Sun is not a planet: it is our nearest star.

fact.text: The light of daytime on Earth comes from our closest star, the Sun!
fact.support: Our daytime Sun is a giant glowing ball of hot plasma, which is a star.

misconception: Thinking the Sun is a gigantic planet because it looks big and round in our daytime sky.

prompt: Tap all the objects that produce their own glowing light!
hint: The Moon does not make light: it reflects light from the Sun!

fact.text: The Moon does not make light; it simply reflects light from the Sun!
fact.support: The Moon produces no light itself; moonlight is sunlight reflecting off its dusty surface.

misconception: Thinking the Moon makes its own light like a glowing lightbulb in the night sky.

prompt: Tap all the giant planets that have rings around them!
hint: Saturn has famous rings, but Jupiter and Uranus have rings too!

fact.text: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune all have rings circling around them in space!
fact.support: Saturn has the most visible rings, but Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune also have ring systems.

misconception: Thinking Saturn is the only planet in our solar system that has rings.

prompt: Order the first four rocky planets starting closest to the Sun!
hint: Start at Mercury, then Venus, our Earth, and red planet Mars.

fact.text: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are inner rocky planets made of dense metals and stone!
fact.support: Mercury is closest to the Sun, followed by Venus, Earth, and Mars in orbital order.

misconception: Thinking Earth is closer to the Sun than Venus because summer feels so warm.

prompt: Order these space neighbors from closest to Earth to furthest!
hint: The Moon orbits Earth, Sun is next, distant stars are furthest.

fact.text: The Moon is about 239,000 miles from Earth. The Sun, our closest star, is about 93 million miles away.
fact.support: The Moon orbits Earth at 238,855 miles away, the Sun is 93 million miles away, and distant stars are 25 trillion miles.

misconception: Thinking stars at night are closer to us than the Moon because they twinkle so brightly.

prompt: Who has more bones inside their skeleton?
hint: Babies start with about 300 bones that fuse together over time!

fact.text: A newborn baby starts with around 300 bones, which fuse into 206 bones in an adult person!
fact.support: Human babies are born with around 300 bones, which gradually fuse into 206 adult bones.

misconception: Thinking bigger adults must have more bones in their skeletons than tiny babies.

prompt: Which is the LARGEST single organ of the human body?
hint: It covers your body from your head all the way to your toes!

fact.text: Skin is the largest organ of the human body, protecting everything inside your body.
fact.support: Skin is the human body's largest organ, forming an outer shield that protects internal parts.

misconception: Thinking skin is just thin wrapping rather than the largest organ of the human body.

prompt: Which is the hardest part of your body?
hint: It forms the tough gleaming shield covering every tooth in your mouth!

fact.text: Tooth enamel is the hardest part of your body, protecting each tooth with a hard mineral shield.
fact.support: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, even tougher than skeleton bones.

misconception: Thinking thick leg bones are the hardest material in the human body.

prompt: Tap all the sensory parts found on your smiling face!
hint: Knees bend for running, but eyes, nose, and tongue explore senses!

fact.text: The tongue has taste buds that detect sweet, salty, sour, savory and bitter tastes!
fact.support: Your tongue has thousands of tiny taste buds that send flavor signals directly to your brain.

misconception: Thinking you taste food with your teeth and lips instead of taste buds on your tongue.

prompt: Order by teeth, fewest to most!
hint: Babies start with zero teeth, toddlers grow twenty baby teeth, and adults have up to thirty-two!

fact.text: Babies usually start with zero teeth, toddlers get 20 baby teeth, and adults can grow up to 32 permanent teeth!
fact.support: Infants start with zero teeth, toddlers grow 20 baby teeth, and adults can have 32 permanent teeth.

misconception: Thinking babies are born with a full set of teeth already in their mouths.

prompt: Order what happens as healthy food journeys through your body!
hint: Teeth chew first, throat swallows, and stomach digests into energy.

fact.text: Your teeth chew meals, which travel through the esophagus into the stomach for digestion!
fact.support: Teeth chew food, the throat swallows it down the esophagus, and the stomach digests it.

misconception: Thinking food drops directly into the stomach without being chewed by teeth first.

prompt: Which creature builds wooden dams to make safe family ponds?
hint: Beavers gnaw trees with orange teeth to build sturdy lodges and dams.
misconception: Thinking beavers build dams just to store food rather than create deep protective ponds.

fact.text: Beavers build stick dams that slow down meadow water. These quiet ponds make safe homes for wildlife!
fact.support: By building dams that form slow-moving ponds, beavers provide wetlands and resources for dozens of wildlife species.

prompt: Tap the wetland homes where wild alligators live!
hint: Alligators thrive in freshwater swamps, marshes, and riverbanks.
misconception: Thinking alligators live in open ocean waves with salty water like dolphins.

fact.text: Alligators are large reptiles that live in freshwater swamps. They can also swim in rivers and lakes!
fact.support: American alligators primarily inhabit freshwater swamps and marshes, though they also swim in rivers and lakes.

prompt: Which plant is the main food of giant pandas?
hint: Pandas spend hours each day happily munching on stalks of bamboo.
misconception: Thinking giant pandas hunt fish or small mammals in the snow like polar bears.

fact.text: Giant pandas eat mostly bamboo. They chew the tough green stalks with strong teeth!
fact.support: Giant pandas have large molar teeth and strong jaw muscles for crushing tough bamboo.

prompt: Which body parts join together to form an elephant's long trunk?
hint: An elephant breathes and smells through its trunk because it is an elongated nose.
misconception: Thinking an elephant's trunk is an extra giant arm or special single muscle.

fact.text: An elephant trunk is a wonderful mix. It joins the nose and upper lip together!
fact.support: An elephant's flexible trunk is actually a wonderful fusion of its nose and upper lip.

prompt: What causes different seasons to cycle throughout the year across our globe?
hint: Earth leans on a slant as it circles around the Sun.
misconception: Thinking summer happens because planet Earth travels closer to the Sun in July.

fact.text: Earth leans on a tilted axis. As our planet orbits the Sun, the tilted lean makes the seasons change!
fact.support: Earth's tilted axis creates our seasons as different regions receive direct solar rays throughout the year.

prompt: Why does our daytime meadow sky appear brightly colored in blue?
hint: Blue light waves scatter in all directions through the gases in our atmosphere.
misconception: Thinking the clear blue sky is just reflecting blue water from the world's oceans.

fact.text: Sunlight holds every rainbow color. Blue light waves scatter across the sky more than other light waves!
fact.support: Sunlight contains all colors, but blue light is scattered more across our atmosphere than other colors.

prompt: Tap the planets that are gas giants without a solid surface!
hint: Jupiter and Saturn have thick clouds with no solid ground underneath.
misconception: Thinking every planet in our solar system has hard ground where you could stand.

fact.text: Jupiter and Saturn are massive gas giants. They have thick cloudy skies without any solid ground to walk on!
fact.support: Jupiter and Saturn are massive gas giants that have thick atmospheres without a solid rocky ground.
evidence: Jupiter and Saturn are massive gas giants

prompt: What is the typical climate on the red surface of Mars?
hint: Mars is much further from the Sun than Earth, making it very chilly.
misconception: Thinking Mars is scorching hot because its rusty red rocks look like glowing flames.

fact.text: Mars is a cold desert world. It sits much farther away from the warm Sun than Earth!
fact.support: Mars is a cold desert world located much farther from the warmth of the Sun.

prompt: Which tireless organ acts like a steady pump inside your chest?
hint: Your heart beats continuously day and night to power circulation throughout your body.
misconception: Thinking lungs pump the blood through your veins instead of breathing in oxygen.

fact.text: Your heart is a tireless muscle pump. It beats day and night to send oxygen through your body!
fact.support: The heart is a muscular pump that delivers oxygen throughout the human body.

prompt: Tap the vital signs doctors check to see how you are doing!
hint: Doctors check how your heart beats and how lungs take in breaths.
misconception: Thinking shoe size or how tall you are counted as medical vital signs.

fact.text: Doctors check vital signs to see how you feel. Your heartbeat and breathing rate show healthy body work!
fact.support: Vital signs reflect essential body functions, including your heartbeat rate and your regular breathing rate.

prompt: Which body part helps you keep your balance?
hint: Deep inside your ear canal is a tiny fluid-filled balance maze.
misconception: Thinking your feet or eyes are the primary organs that detect body balance.

fact.text: Tiny fluid canals inside your inner ear sense head motion. They send balance signals to your brain!
fact.support: Some balance problems are due to problems in the inner ear.

prompt: Order these organs as swallowed food moves down!
hint: Food moves from your throat into the stomach, and then enters the intestines.
misconception: Thinking food drops into the intestines before reaching the acid in your stomach.

fact.text: Swallowed food moves down your throat passage. Powerful acid breaks meals down inside your stomach and intestines!
fact.support: Swallowed food travels through the digestive tract, moving from throat into stomach and intestines.

prompt: Order how parent eagles raise a new family from start to finish!
hint: Think about what parent eagles build before laying their eggs.

fact.text: Parent eagles build big stick nests. They keep their eggs warm until little chicks hatch!
fact.support: Parent eagles construct large stick nests, incubate their laid eggs, and raise hatched chicks together.
evidence: Eagles construct their nests near water in tall trees or on cliffs using large sticks

misconception: Children sometimes think birds find ready-made nests, but parents carefully build a nest before laying eggs.

prompt: Which creature is a giant living lizard?
hint: One of these scaly creatures is the world's largest living lizard.

fact.text: Komodo dragons are giant lizards. They have long tails, strong legs, and agile necks!
fact.support: Komodo dragons are large lizards with long tails, strong agile necks, and sturdy limbs.
evidence: Komodo dragons are large lizards with long tails, strong and agile necks, and sturdy limbs

misconception: Children often confuse dragons with make-believe fantasy beasts, but Komodo dragons are real giant lizards.

prompt: Tap all the wild animals that hunt together in teams!
hint: Two of these animals cooperate in packs or prides to find food.

fact.text: Gray wolves hunt together in packs. African lions also team up in prides to catch food!
fact.support: Gray wolves hunt in packs, and African lions team up in prides to catch prey together.

misconception: Children often believe big predators always hunt as solitary loners, but wolves and lions hunt in coordinated teams.

prompt: Which speedy cat has special running claws that act like cleats?
hint: Think about which spotted sprinter needs non-slip traction to run fast.

fact.text: Cheetahs sprint across open ground with great speed. Special paw claws dig into soil like running cleats!
fact.support: Special paw pads and semi-retractable claws provide cheetahs great traction while running.

misconception: Children often think all cats retract their claws fully into paws, but cheetah claws stay out for running grip.

prompt: Put these Moon shapes in order, from new to full!
hint: A new moon is dark before a sliver crescent grows into a full glowing circle.

fact.text: As the Moon orbits Earth, we see more sunlit shapes. It grows from a new moon to a full moon!
fact.support: Starting at the new moon, a waxing crescent appears, and grows into a bright full moon.

misconception: Children sometimes think the Moon physically changes shape or grows, but we just see different lighted angles.

prompt: Tap the ice giants!
hint: The two coldest outer gas planets contain deep icy slush layers.

fact.text: Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. They hold water, ammonia and methane. Scientists call these fluids ices!
fact.support: Uranus is made of water, methane, and ammonia fluids above a small rocky center.

misconception: Children often classify all four outer planets simply as gas giants, but Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

prompt: Which distant planet is famous for being dark, cold, and very windy?
hint: This deep blue planet has supersonic icy storms and faint rings.

fact.text: Neptune is a dark and windy world. It circles far away from the warm light of our Sun!
fact.support: Neptune is a very cold, windy world encircled by thin rings far away from the Sun.
evidence: Neptune is a very cold, windy world

misconception: Children might think wind only blows on Earth with trees, but supersonic icy winds howl on Neptune.

prompt: Tap the rocky worlds with a solid surface to walk on!
hint: Select the two rocky worlds with solid ground underfoot.

fact.text: Mercury and Earth are rocky worlds. Both planets have solid surfaces of metal and stone!
fact.support: Mercury and Earth are terrestrial planets with compact rocky crusts.

misconception: Children sometimes think all planets are made of gas like Jupiter, but inner planets are solid rock.

prompt: Tap the nerve tissues found inside your brain!
hint: Look for the two shades of nerve tissue that fill your thinking cap.

fact.text: Your brain contains gray matter made of cell bodies. It also has white matter made of nerve fibers.
fact.support: The tissue called "gray matter" in the brain and spinal cord is also known as substantia grisea, and is made up of cell bodies.

misconception: Thinking the brain is one single solid block of gray jelly without distinct nerve layers.

prompt: Which inner eye part changes shape to focus incoming light rays?
hint: This clear part behind the pupil flexes to focus your sight.

fact.text: The flexible lens inside your eye changes shape to focus light. Your pupil changes size to adjust light!
fact.support: The lens itself is flexible and suspended by ligaments which allow it to change shape to focus light on the retina.

misconception: Children often believe eyes just project sight like flashlights, but the flexible lens focuses light onto the sensitive retina inside.

prompt: Order how fresh breaths travel deeper into your lungs!
hint: Follow breath from the windpipe down into branching tubes and air sacs.

fact.text: Fresh air travels down your windpipe into branch tubes. It enters tiny air sacs called alveoli.
fact.support: The major respiratory structures include the windpipe, which branches into bronchial tubes and tiny alveoli air sacs.
evidence: bronchial tubes and tiny alveoli air sacs

misconception: Children often imagine air sits in one big hollow bag, but airway passages branch into millions of microscopic sacs.

prompt: Tap all the vital chest organs sheltered inside your curved rib cage!
hint: Your sturdy rib bones wrap around two vital chest organs.

fact.text: Your curved rib cage acts like a bone shield. It shelters both your spongy lungs and your beating heart!
fact.support: Your curved rib cage acts like a protective shield around your chest to shelter both your lungs and heart.
evidence: shelter both your lungs and heart

misconception: Children sometimes think ribs are just rigid sticks, but together they form an elastic protective cage shielding internal chest organs.

prompt: How do elephants drink water with their long trunk?
hint: Elephants take water into their trunk and spray it into their mouth.

fact.text: Elephants do not drink through their trunk like a straw. They suck water into the trunk and squirt it into their mouths!
fact.support: Elephants use their trunks to take up water and squirt it into their mouths.

misconception: Children often think elephants drink directly through their trunks like a giant drinking straw.

prompt: Tap all the mammals with webbed feet or swimming eye shields!
hint: Look for two meadow mammals built with specialized swimming features.

fact.text: River otters have clear eye shields for swimming. Beavers use large webbed feet to paddle through water!
fact.support: River otters have clear protective eye membranes, and beavers possess large webbed hind feet for swimming.

misconception: Children sometimes think all mammals swim poorly like cats, but otters and beavers are expert aquatic swimmers.

prompt: Which creature closes its nostrils to suck up termites?
hint: This shaggy animal uses its specialized snout to suck up termites and ants.

fact.text: A sloth bear can close its nostrils to keep out dust and insects while it sucks up termites.
fact.support: Sloth bears' nostrils can close completely, protecting the animals from dust or insects when raiding termite nests or beehives.

misconception: Children often believe all bears eat honey or salmon, but sloth bears specialize in vacuuming up termites.

prompt: Order how a frog grows up from start to finish!
hint: Follow the frog transformation from egg to swimmer to adult.

fact.text: Amphibian eggs hatch in fresh water. Little tadpoles swim and grow legs until they become adult frogs!
fact.support: Eggs laid in water hatch quickly, swim as tadpoles, and transform into grown adult frogs.

misconception: Children sometimes think baby frogs hatch looking like miniature frogs with four legs, but they start as legless swimming tadpoles.

prompt: Line them up from the Sun to the Earth during a solar eclipse!
hint: Line them up from the star, to the shadow-maker, to the planet.

fact.text: During an eclipse, the Sun shines. The Moon moves between. Earth receives the dark shadow!
fact.support: Sunlight begins at the Sun, passes the Moon, and falls upon Earth.

misconception: Children often think the Sun turns off, but the Moon simply passes directly between Earth and Sun.

prompt: Which planet spins backward compared to Earth?
hint: This bright yellowish planet turns slowly in reverse compared to our home world.

fact.text: Venus spins backward in slow motion. It turns in the opposite way from Earth across cloudy skies!
fact.support: Venus spins the opposite direction of Earth and most other planets.
evidence: spins the opposite direction of earth

misconception: Children expect all solar system planets to rotate the same way, but Venus rotates backward.

prompt: Order these space zones traveling outward from our Sun!
hint: Remember the rocky asteroid ring sits between the red planet and the largest gas giant.

fact.text: The asteroid belt is a rocky zone in space. It orbits between the paths of Mars and giant Jupiter!
fact.support: Swallowed food moves from the throat passage to the stomach and intestines.

misconception: Children sometimes think asteroids are scattered randomly everywhere, but most orbit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.

prompt: What happens to your body on a world with smaller mass than Earth?
hint: Less gravity pulls down on you when a world has less mass.

fact.text: Worlds with smaller mass have weaker gravity. A world with less mass pulls you with less force, so you weigh less!
fact.support: If you were on a planet with less mass than Earth, you would weigh less than you do here.
evidence: weigh less than you do here

misconception: Children often think you weigh the same everywhere in space, but weaker gravity makes you weigh less.

prompt: Tap the soft tissues found inside human bone cores!
hint: Select the two warm colors that describe real bone marrow.

fact.text: Human bones contain red marrow to make new cells. They also hold yellow marrow made mostly of fat.
fact.support: Bone marrow is the spongy tissue inside some of your bones, such as your hip and thigh bones.
evidence: Bone marrow is the spongy tissue

misconception: Children often imagine bone marrow is just one plain grey substance, but it comes in distinct red and yellow forms.

prompt: Which solid bone helmet shelters your brain from bumps and falls?
hint: This round cranial bone encases your thoughts like an armor helmet.

fact.text: Your hard skull bone acts like a sturdy helmet. It protects your delicate brain from bumps!
fact.support: Often, the injury is minor because your skull is hard and it protects your brain.

misconception: Children sometimes think the skull is just for facial shape, but its primary purpose is a helmet shielding the brain.

prompt: Order the layers of an arm or leg bone from outside inward!
hint: Work inward from the tough exterior shell down to the central cavity.

fact.text: A bone has dense compact bone on the outside. It has porous spongy bone inside and soft marrow at the center.
fact.support: From the outside in, a skeleton bone has hard compact outer bone, airy spongy mesh, and soft marrow.
evidence: airy spongy mesh, and soft marrow

misconception: Children sometimes think bones are solid white rock all the way through, but they contain porous spongy tissue and soft marrow inside.

prompt: What happens to your brain while you are fast asleep at night?
hint: Even when dreaming, your brain continues sorting memories and guiding your body.

fact.text: Your brain does not shut off at night. While you are sleeping, your brain and body functions remain active!
fact.support: While you are sleeping your brain and body functions are still active.

misconception: Thinking your brain completely turns off or shuts down like a computer during sleep.
